title: Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Issues
subject: Biology
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: What is Biodiversity? Define the 3 hierarchical levels of diversity (Edward Wilson).
cards.a:
Biodiversity: The totality of genes, species, and ecosystems of a given region (popularized by sociobiologist Edward Wilson):
1. Genetic Diversity: Diversity of genes within a single species (e.g. Rauwolfia vomitoria producing varying potency of reserpine; India has >50,000 genetically different strains of rice and >1,000 varieties of mango).
2. Species Diversity: Variety of species within a region (e.g. Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than Eastern Ghats).
3. Ecological / Ecosystem Diversity: Diversity of habitats and ecosystems (e.g. India has deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs, alpine meadows).
cards.hint: Rauwolfia vomitoria exhibits genetic diversity in the concentration of medicinal alkaloid Reserpine.

cards.q: Global Species Diversity: Robert May's Estimate and Taxonomic Breakdown?
cards.a:
IUCN Red List (2004) documents ~1.5 million described species.
Robert May's scientifically sound global estimate = ~7 MILLION species worldwide.
Taxonomic Proportions:
- Animals constitute >70% of all recorded species; Plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms) comprise ~22%.
- Among animals, INSECTS are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up >70% of all animals (7 out of every 10 animals are insects!).
- The number of Fungi species in the world exceeds the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals!
cards.hint: Over 70% of all species are animals; over 70% of all animals are insects.

cards.q: India's Megadiversity Status: Exact percentages and global standing?
cards.a:
India is one of the 12 Mega-Diversity countries of the world:
- Land Area: India occupies ONLY 2.4% of the world's total land area.
- Global Species Share: India contributes an impressive 8.1% of global species diversity!
- Documented Species in India: ~45,000 species of plants and ~90,000 to 100,000 species of animals.
- If May's estimate applies, over 100,000 plant species and 300,000 animal species are yet to be discovered in India.
cards.hint: India has 2.4% of world land area, but 8.1% of global species diversity!

cards.q: Latitudinal Gradients of Biodiversity: Why are Tropics richest in species?
cards.a:
Species diversity decreases progressively from equator towards the poles (Tropics $23.5^\circ$N to $23.5^\circ$S harbor maximum species; e.g. Amazonian rainforest is the richest).
3 Evolutionary Reasons:
1. Constant, Predictable Climate: Tropics have less seasonal variation, promoting niche specialization and speciation.
2. Undisturbed Evolutionary Time: Tropics remained undisturbed by glaciations for millions of years (unlike temperate regions subjected to frequent glaciations).
3. Higher Solar Energy: More solar insolation fuels higher productivity, indirectly supporting greater diversity.
cards.hint: Equator to poles = decreasing species diversity. Colombia near equator has 1,400 bird species; Greenland at 71°N has only 56.

cards.q: Species-Area Relationship (Alexander von Humboldt): Equation and Z-values?
cards.a:
Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area up to a limit (produces a Rectangular Hyperbola).
Logarithmic equation: $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$
Where:
- $S$: Species richness, $A$: Area, $C$: Y-intercept
- $Z$: Slope of regression line (regression coefficient)
Values of $Z$:
- For normal small regions (plants in Britain, birds in California): $Z = 0.1 \text{ to } 0.2$.
- For very large areas (entire continents): $Z = 0.6 \text{ to } 1.2$ (much steeper slope).
- For Frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of continents: $Z = 1.15$.
cards.hint: On a logarithmic scale, the species-area rectangular hyperbola becomes a straight line.

cards.q: Importance of Species Diversity: David Tilman's Experiments and Rivet Popper Hypothesis?
cards.a:
1. David Tilman's Outdoor Plot Experiments: Plots with higher species richness showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and displayed higher overall productivity, proving diversity promotes ecosystem stability.
2. Paul Ehrlich's 'Rivet Popper Hypothesis':
- Airplane = Ecosystem; Rivets = Species.
- If passengers pop rivets (extinction), initial loss of a few rivets on seats does not endanger flight immediately.
- But popping key rivets on the WINGS (keystone species, e.g. pollinators, top predators) directly threatens the structural integrity and flight safety of the airplane (ecosystem collapse).
cards.hint: Loss of a keystone species causes catastrophic disruption of the entire ecosystem.

cards.q: Loss of Biodiversity: 'The Evil Quartet' (4 Major Causes of Extinction)?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: 'The Evil Quartet' (Jared Diamond):
1. Habitat Loss and Fragmentation: Most dangerous driver (e.g. Amazon rainforest 'Lungs of the planet' slashed and burned for soybean cultivation; cleared from 14% to <6%).
2. Over-Exploitation: Commercial greed (Steller's Sea Cow, Passenger Pigeon, Dodo driven to extinction by excessive hunting).
3. Alien / Invasive Species Invasions: Displacement of indigenous species (Nile Perch, Water Hyacinth, Parthenium).
4. Co-Extinctions: When a host species becomes extinct, its obligate dependent parasites and mutualists also go extinct.
cards.hint: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the number one cause driving animals and plants to extinction.

cards.q: Invasive Alien Species: Nile Perch, Water Hyacinth, Parthenium, and African Catfish?
cards.a:
Non-native species that multiply aggressively and displace native flora/fauna:
1. Nile Perch: Introduced into Lake Victoria (East Africa); caused extinction of an entire endemic assemblage of >200 species of native Cichlid fish.
2. Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes / 'Terror of Bengal'): Clogs waterways, blocks light, and depletes dissolved oxygen, killing native aquatic life.
3. Carrot Grass (Parthenium hysterophorus) & Lantana camara: Aggressive invasive weeds choking indigenous pastureland.
4. African Catfish (Clarias gariepinus): Illegally introduced for aquaculture; poses grave threat to indigenous Indian catfishes.
cards.hint: Eichhornia was introduced to India for its lovely mauve flowers and leaf shape, but turned into an ecological disaster.

cards.q: In-Situ (On-Site) Conservation: Biosphere Reserves, National Parks, and Sanctuaries?
cards.a:
Conserving endangered species within their natural habitat:
1. Biosphere Reserves: Multipurpose protected areas with Core (undisturbed), Buffer (limited research), and Transition zones (human settlement); 14 in India (e.g. Nilgiri, Sundarbans).
2. National Parks: Strict government protection; private ownership, grazing, and forestry are completely prohibited; 90 in India (e.g. Jim Corbett, Kaziranga - one-horned rhino).
3. Wildlife Sanctuaries: Protection of animals; controlled human activities (timber harvesting, minor forest produce) permitted; 448 in India.
4. Sacred Groves: Undisturbed forest patches protected on religious grounds (Khasi and Jaintia hills Meghalaya, Aravalli hills Rajasthan, Western Ghats).
cards.hint: In national parks, human activities and cattle grazing are strictly banned; in wildlife sanctuaries, controlled human activity is permitted.

cards.q: Ex-Situ (Off-Site) Conservation: Zoological Parks, Botanical Gardens, and Cryopreservation?
cards.a:
Protecting threatened animals and plants outside their natural habitats in specialized artificial facilities with care:
1. Zoological Parks and Botanical Gardens: Preserving live specimens for breeding, research, and education.
2. Wildlife Safari Parks: Animals kept in large enclosures resembling natural habitats.
3. Cryopreservation: Storing gametes of threatened species in viable and fertile condition at ultra-low temperature of -196°C in Liquid Nitrogen indefinitely.
4. Seed Banks / Gene Banks: Storing seeds of diverse strains in viable conditions.
5. In Vitro Tissue Culture propagation.
cards.hint: Cryopreservation at -196°C in liquid nitrogen allows indefinite preservation of viable gametes.

cards.q: Biodiversity Hotspots: Norman Myers' criteria, global count, and Hotspots in India?
cards.a:
Regions characterized by exceptionally high species richness and high degree of Endemism (species confined strictly to that region and found nowhere else), under severe threat of habitat destruction.
- Total Hotspots: Originally 25, now 36 worldwide (cover <2% of Earth's land, but harbor >50% terrestrial species; strict protection could reduce ongoing extinction by 30%).
3 Hotspots covering India:
1. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka
2. Indo-Burma (covers Northeast India excluding Assam)
3. Himalaya (entire Himalayan mountain range).
cards.hint: Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya are the 3 major biodiversity hotspots covering India.

cards.q: International Biodiversity Summits: Earth Summit vs World Summit?
cards.a:
1. The Earth Summit (Historic Convention on Biological Diversity - CBD):
- Held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil in 1992.
- Called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilization of its benefits.
2. The World Summit on Sustainable Development:
- Held in Johannesburg, South Africa in 2002.
- 190 countries pledged their commitment to achieve a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.
cards.hint: Earth Summit = Rio de Janeiro, 1992; World Summit = Johannesburg, 2002.

cards.q: Air Pollution: Electrostatic Precipitator and Scrubber mechanism?
cards.a:
Devices controlling industrial air emissions:
1. Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP):
- Removes over 99% of particulate matter from thermal power plant exhaust.
- Electrode wires maintained at several thousand volts generate a corona that releases electrons $\rightarrow$ particles acquire negative charge $\rightarrow$ attracted to positively charged grounded collecting plates $\rightarrow$ clean air exits.
2. Scrubber:
- Removes harmful gases like Sulfur Dioxide ($SO_2$) from exhaust by passing dirty gas through a spray of water or Lime ($Ca(OH)_2$) slurry.
cards.hint: Electrostatic Precipitator removes >99% particulate matter; Scrubber cleans gaseous $SO_2$.

cards.q: CPCB Guidelines on Particulate Matter and Catalytic Converters?
cards.a:
1. CPCB (Central Pollution Control Board) Standard:
- Particulate matter of size PM 2.5 (diameter 2.5 micrometers or less) is the MOST HARMFUL to human health; can be inhaled deep into bronchioles and alveoli, causing chronic respiratory inflammation, lung damage, and premature death.
2. Catalytic Converters in Automobiles:
- Fitted with expensive precious metal catalysts: Platinum-Palladium and Rhodium.
- Converts unburnt hydrocarbons $\rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O$; Carbon monoxide ($CO$) $\rightarrow CO_2$; Nitric oxide ($NO$) $\rightarrow N_2$ gas.
- Vehicles must strictly use UNLEADED petrol (lead poisons and inactivates the catalysts).
cards.hint: Lead in leaded petrol permanently inactivates the platinum/rhodium catalyst in catalytic converters.

cards.q: Air and Water Pollution Legislation in India (Acts and amendments)?
cards.a:
1. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act: Enacted in 1974 to safeguard water resources.
2. Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act: Enacted in 1981.
- Amended in 1987 to include NOISE as an air pollutant (brief exposure to >150 dB sound, e.g. jet takeoff, permanently impairs hearing).
3. Environment (Protection) Act: Enacted in 1986 to protect and improve the quality of environment (air, water, soil).
cards.hint: Noise was legally incorporated as an air pollutant under the Air Act amendment of 1987.

cards.q: Biomagnification of DDT in Aquatic Food Chains?
cards.a:
Biomagnification: Progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable, toxic, fat-soluble substances at successive trophic levels of a food chain.
Classic DDT Aquatic Cascade:
1. Water: 0.003 ppb (parts per billion)
2. Zooplankton: 0.04 ppm (parts per million)
3. Small Fish: 0.5 ppm
4. Large Fish: 2 ppm
5. Fish-eating Birds (Pelicans, Ospreys): 25 ppm! (Concentration magnified ~10 million times!).
Toxic effect: High DDT interferes with calcium metabolism, causing thinning of eggshells and premature breaking, leading to catastrophic bird population decline.
cards.hint: Top carnivores (fish-eating birds) accumulate the highest concentration of toxic DDT.

cards.q: Eutrophication: Natural vs Cultural (Accelerated) Eutrophication?
cards.a:
Eutrophication: Natural aging of a lake by biological nutrient enrichment of its water (water becomes shallow and warm over centuries).
Cultural / Accelerated Eutrophication:
- Runoff containing agricultural fertilizers (nitrates and phosphates) and municipal sewage into water bodies massively accelerates nutrient enrichment.
- Causes explosive ALGAL BLOOMS (massive proliferation of planktonic algae) $\rightarrow$ covers water surface $\rightarrow$ blocks light $\rightarrow$ algae die $\rightarrow$ aerobic decomposers consume all dissolved oxygen $\rightarrow$ massive fish mortality and water body asphyxiation.
cards.hint: Algal blooms impart distinct odors and colors and choke aquatic life by exhausting dissolved oxygen.

cards.q: Ecological Sanitation (EcoSan Toilets) and Integrated Wastewater Treatment (Arcata)?
cards.a:
1. EcoSan Toilets: Sustainable, dry composting toilets that handle human excreta without water; hygienic, cost-effective, and converts human waste into sterile organic fertilizer (used in Kerala and Sri Lanka).
2. Arcata Town Wastewater Treatment (California & Humboldt State University):
- Integrated 2-stage system:
  - Stage 1: Conventional sedimentation, filtration, and chlorine treatment.
  - Stage 2: Marshland series (6 connected marshes over 60 hectares) seeded with algae, fungi, bacteria, and reeds that naturally assimilate and neutralize heavy metals and toxins.
cards.hint: EcoSan toilets eliminate water wastage and recycle human excreta into safe agricultural manure.

cards.q: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming: Relative contribution of Greenhouse Gases?
cards.a:
Greenhouse effect: Naturally occurring thermal phenomenon that keeps Earth surface warm (~15°C instead of freezing -18°C).
Enhanced Greenhouse Effect causes Global Warming (Earth's temperature rose by 0.6°C in 20th century).
Relative Contribution of Greenhouse Gases (Pie Chart):
1. Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$): 60%
2. Methane ($CH_4$): 20%
3. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs): 14%
4. Nitrous Oxide ($N_2O$): 6%
Consequences: Polar ice cap melting, sea level rise, submerged coastal plains, El Niño weather abnormalities.
cards.hint: Memorize the exact gas contribution: $CO_2$ (60%), $CH_4$ (20%), CFCs (14%), $N_2O$ (6%).

cards.q: Ozone Depletion in Stratosphere: 'Good Ozone' vs 'Bad Ozone' and Dobson Units?
cards.a:
1. Bad Ozone: Formed in TROPOSPHERE (lower atmosphere); acts as a toxic air pollutant harming plants and animals.
2. Good Ozone: Present in STRATOSPHERE (upper atmosphere); absorbs lethal UV-B radiation (causes skin cancer, cataracts, DNA damage).
Measurement: Thickness of ozone layer is measured in DOBSON UNITS (DU).
Depletion Mechanism:
- CFCs released from refrigerators diffuse into stratosphere $\rightarrow$ UV rays break CFCs, releasing free CHLORINE ($Cl^\bullet$) atoms.
- Chlorine acts as a catalyst: $Cl^\bullet + O_3 \rightarrow ClO + O_2$; regenerated $Cl$ atom continues to destroy thousands of ozone molecules (Ozone Hole over Antarctica).
cards.hint: One single chlorine radical ($Cl^\bullet$) can catalytically destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules!

cards.q: Montreal Protocol (1987) for Ozone Layer Protection?
cards.a:
Historic international environmental treaty signed in Montreal, Canada in 1987 (effective in 1989):
- Aim: Control and phase out the production and consumption of Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS), primarily Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons, and carbon tetrachloride.
- Widely hailed as the most successful international environmental treaty in history, resulting in measurable recovery of the Antarctic stratospheric ozone layer.
cards.hint: Montreal Protocol = Protection of Stratospheric Ozone layer (signed 1987, effective 1989).

cards.q: Deforestation: Causes and Slash & Burn Agriculture (Jhum Cultivation)?
cards.a:
Deforestation: Conversion of forested areas into non-forest lands (at the start of 20th century, forests covered 30% of India; shrunk to 21.54% by end of century; National Forest Policy 1988 recommends 33% forest cover for plains and 67% for hills).
Jhum Cultivation (Slash and Burn Agriculture) in Northeast India:
- Farmers cut forest trees, burn the plant remains, and use ash as fertilizer for crop farming.
- In earlier times, long fallow periods allowed natural forest recovery; with population explosion, repeated cycling without fallow time causes catastrophic deforestation and soil erosion.
cards.hint: National Forest Policy (1988) recommends 33% forest cover for plains and 67% for hilly terrain.

cards.q: People's Movements in Forest Conservation: Amrita Devi Bishnoi, Chipko Movement, and JFM?
cards.a:
1. Amrita Devi Bishnoi (1731, Rajasthan): In Khejarli village near Jodhpur, Amrita Devi and her 3 daughters hugged Khejri trees to protect them from king's axe-men; sacrificed their lives along with 363 Bishnois. Govt. of India instituted the 'Amrita Devi Bishnoi National Award for Wildlife Protection'.
2. Chipko Movement (1974, Garhwal Himalayas): Local women hugged forest trees to prevent commercial logging by contractors (led by Sunderlal Bahuguna).
3. Joint Forest Management (JFM, 1980s): Govt. initiative partnering with local communities to manage and protect degraded forests; communities receive non-wood forest products in return.
cards.hint: Bishnoi movement protected Khejri trees (Prosopis cineraria) in Rajasthan in 1731.

cards.q: Solid Waste Management: Sanitary Landfills and Ahmed Khan's Polyblend?
cards.a:
1. Sanitary Landfills: Waste dumped in depressions and covered with dirt daily; limitations: seepage of toxic chemicals (leachate) pollutes underground drinking water; methane explosion hazard.
2. Ahmed Khan's Polyblend (Bangalore, 1998):
- Developed Polyblend, a fine recycled powder of modified plastic waste.
- Mixed Polyblend with Bitumen (asphalt) in 1:9 ratio to lay roads.
- Roads with Polyblend have 3 times longer lifespan and enhanced water-repellent properties, providing a sustainable solution to plastic waste.
cards.hint: Ahmed Khan demonstrated that recycled plastic waste (Polyblend) blended with bitumen makes superior roads.
